extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of Florentine history and political theory (Machiavelli-related)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting normative principles and institutional lessons about causes of stability and instability in republican Florence (late 14th–early 15th century), as discussed in a historical/political narrative. Useful for historical-political analysis and comparative constitutional observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of change in republics
rubrics_metrics.description: "All republics, especially such as are not well constituted, undergo frequent changes in their laws and manner of government; and this is not owing to the nature either of liberty or subjection in general ... It is, indeed, oppression and licence that occasion changes; but where the constitution is good, the laws govern, and prevent oppression as well as licence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a republic's stability by checking for two pathologies: (1) oppression (excessive domination by a party/elite) and (2) unbridled licentiousness (lawlessness of populace). A well-constituted system with genuine liberty and true obedience tends to preserve constancy; reforms should aim to reduce oppression and licence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of unequal guilds/arts causing faction
rubrics_metrics.description: Division into arts produced distinctions (seven greater arts, fourteen lesser), and "because some were more and others less honourable... they came by degrees to be distinguished" which "chiefly gave occasion to all those tumults".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When corporate or guild-based institutions are given unequal honors or power, favoritism fosters factional arrogance and civil disturbance. Institutional design should avoid rigid favoritism among occupational groups and ensure balanced privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of recourse for unincorporated/meaner trades
rubrics_metrics.description: Many trades not incorporated had no other head to apply to for redress but the magistrate of the company to which the person employed them, who they commonly thought did not do them justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide accessible mechanisms for grievances and redress for lesser or unincorporated economic groups; absence of legitimate channels drives nocturnal meetings, agitation, and potential revolt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective impunity encourages escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: "To come off with impunity for our past offences, it is necessary to add still more to them, to redouble our outrages... for where many are guilty none are chastised. Small crimes are punished, and great ones usually rewarded... To redouble our crimes is the surest way to procure a pardon."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to strategic logic within mobs: perceived collective impunity incentivizes escalation. Policy should avoid incentives that make mass crimes a path to pardons or concessions; enforce individual accountability to deter mass criminality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fickleness and caprice of popular support
rubrics_metrics.description: The multitude's behaviour was "very curious"—they knighted some citizens whose houses they had burned hours earlier; "Such is the caprice of the multitude, and so soon are their disgusts changed into favour and affection."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume durable popular loyalty; public opinion can be volatile and capricious. Political strategies that rely on sustained mob allegiance risk sudden reversal; institutional stability should not depend on fickle popular passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural necessity for law-making (checks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a law could be passed, it was necessary it should have the assent of the common-council, as well as of the signori; it was contrary to established custom for two councils to be held on the same day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural safeguards (dual assent, separation of deliberations) function as checks on rash or coercive legislation. Maintaining established legislative procedures preserves legitimacy; manipulating meeting schedules or bypassing assent undermines lawful governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repressive measures breed fear and further unrest
rubrics_metrics.description: Executions and banishments abounded; magistrates made new laws to strengthen their hands, which multiplied discontents. "They ... lived in perpetual fear and alarm" and the severity "only served to multiply their discontents, and to increase instead of allaying their own fears."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heavy-handed repression (mass executions, banishments, arbitrary laws) may temporarily secure power but increases suspicion, fear, and long-term instability. Restraint and lawful processes reduce cycles of retaliation and factional revenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced composition of magistracy to prevent domination
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision for signori: five of the body should be drawn out of the less companies, and four out of the greater, and the standard-bearer alternately out of each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design magistracies with representational balance across social/economic factions to limit domination by one group. Explicit quotas or alternating offices can reduce concentration of power and pacify rival interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of leaders influences republican fate
rubrics_metrics.description: Michael di Lando "showed himself in valour, generosity, and prudence" and thereby "well deserves to be reckoned among those few that have been real benefactors to their country. If he had been of an ambitious or self-interested disposition, the republic must have relapsed into a more intolerable degree of servitude."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess leaders not only by office but by personal integrity; virtuous, prudent leaders can stabilize republics, while ambitious/self-interested ones may convert crises into tyranny. Leadership selection and accountability matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite jealousy and creation of extraordinary councils (balia) risks abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Jealousy among elites led to creating a balia to secure the state, by which many citizens were banished or admonished and new imborfations of magistrates made; such measures were used to diminish plebeian authority and promote elite advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extraordinary councils or emergency bodies (balia) established for security can be instruments of partisan exclusion if not checked. Institutional responses to crises should include safeguards against elite capture and permanent curtailment of rivals' rights.
